title: Pastoral Days; or, Memories of a New England Year
description: "Pastoral Days; or, Memories of a New England Year" by W. Hamilton Gibson is a collection of reflective essays written in the late 19th century. The work captures the essence of the changing seasons in New England, providing rich, descriptive accounts of rural life and the natural beauty of the landscape. The author conveys a deep appreciation for the cycle of seasons, intricately detailing personal memories of spring, summer, autumn, and winter, which evoke a sense of nostalgia and connection to nature.  The opening of the book introduces an evocative portrayal of the transition from winter to spring in New England. Gibson observes the landscape covered in snow, highlighting the contrasts and playful caprices of March weather as it signals the coming of spring. He reflects on the life that stirs beneath the surface, from thawing landscapes to the awakening flora and fauna, each element imbued with personal reminiscences. As he recounts the excitement of a spring freshet and the joyous return of wildlife, readers are invited into the vibrant tapestry of memory and experience that shapes his connection to the land. This passage sets the tone for a rich exploration of the natural world through the lens of personal and seasonal changes.

Looking through the dingy window between the maple boughs, my eye extends over lawn and shrubberies, three acres in extent--a little park, overrun with paths in every direction, through ancient orchard and embowered dells, while far beyond are glimpses of the wooded knolls, the winding brook, and meadows dotted with waving willows, and farther still the ample undulating farm.

The old gray toll-bridge soon nears to view, with its two long spans and fantastic beams. Farther on, peering from its willows, stands the ruined cider-mill, with its long moss-grown lever jutting through the trees--an old-time haunt, now crumbling in decay.

“No, sir,” replied Mr. Snug, with a beaming smile and a bow of the head. “This is a lovely morning for contrite meditation. Go--instantly.”

But I believe we were on the road to that carding-mill. We had almost forgotten it; and now, as we look ahead, we see the old lumber-shed that marks the upper ledge of Devil’s Hollow. The final leaf is torn from the tree. The lingering birds depart the desolation for scenes more tranquil, and I too with them, for nothing here invites my tarrying. The Autumn days are gone, grim Winter is at our door, and the covering snow will soon enshroud the earth, subdued and silent in its winter sleep.
